Hints 4 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Count first with a Counter.

Hint 2

Then order by two things: count descending, then word ascending. The trick is the sort key (-count, word): negating the count turns "highest first" into an ascending sort, and the word breaks ties alphabetically in the same ascending sort.

Hint 3

Sorting all distinct words is O(m log m). heapq.nsmallest(k, ..., key=(-count, word)) keeps only k candidates: O(m log k), better when k is small.

Hint 4

This exact question is common for DE roles because it is "GROUP BY word ORDER BY count DESC, word ASC LIMIT k".

In plain words

Doubling the string lines up all its rotations next to each other.

Hints 3 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

A palindrome is pairs mirrored around an optional middle. Every pair of equal letters can be placed on both sides. At most one single letter can sit in the middle.

Hint 2

So: count each letter, add count // 2 * 2 (all its pairs), and if any letter had an odd count, add 1 for the middle.

Hint 3

Like paper multiplication. Multiply every digit pair, add into a result array, and push carries left.

Hints 4 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Shortcut (not allowed): str(int(num1) * int(num2)). Mention it.

Hint 2

Paper multiplication: digit i of num1 times digit j of num2 (counting from the right) contributes to position i + j of the result. The product of an m-digit and an n-digit number has at most m + n digits.

Hint 3

Algorithm: make an array res of m + n zeros. For each pair of digits, add their product into res[i + j + 1] (indexing from the left), push the carry into res[i + j]. Finally strip leading zeros.

Hint 4

Why it is asked: it checks careful index arithmetic, a carry loop, and edge cases like "0".

Two Pointers

Use two indexes that move through the data instead of a nested loop. Turns many O(n²) problems into O(n) with O(1) extra memory.

⇆
Think of it like this

Two people searching a sorted bookshelf from opposite ends. If the pair of books they hold is too light, the left person steps right to a heavier book; too heavy, the right person steps left. Neither ever needs to walk back.

With sorted data, one comparison tells you which side can be thrown away for good. Each step discards one element, so the whole thing finishes in one pass without a nested loop.

Watch the pattern

Spot it in a question

sorted arraypair / tripletfrom both endsin place, O(1) spacemerge two sortedpalindrome

The template

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to sort first.
  • Using <= instead of < and pairing an element with itself.
  • Not skipping duplicates when unique answers are required (3Sum).

Practise this pattern (10 questions)

EValid PalindromeMTwo Sum II (Sorted Input)M3SumMContainer With Most WaterEMove ZeroesEMerge Sorted ArrayERemove Duplicates from Sorted ArrayMSort Colors (Dutch National Flag)ESquares of a Sorted ArrayHTrapping Rain Water
Concept video in Telugu SRK Codes channel ↗
▶Two Pointer Technique | Fast-Slow, Left-Right PointersSRK Codes · Telugu · Python

Deeper notes

When to use it

  • The input is sorted (or you can sort it) and you look for a pair.
  • You compare things from both ends (palindromes, reversing).
  • You merge two sorted sequences.
  • You must modify an array in place.

Pattern 1: pointers from both ends

Find two numbers in a sorted list that add up to a target. If the sum is too small, move the left pointer right (bigger number). If too big, move the right pointer left.

O(n) time, O(1) space. The brute force (check every pair) is O(n²).

Pattern 2: slow and fast pointers (in-place)

Remove duplicates from a sorted list in place. slow marks where the next unique value goes; fast scans.

Pattern 3: merging two sorted lists

Connect the dots

merge_sorted is how a sort-merge join works in Spark: both sides are sorted by the join key, then two pointers walk forward together. It is also how you combine two date-ordered files without loading and re-sorting everything.

Interview angle

Ask "is the input sorted?" early. If yes, two pointers or binary search is almost certainly the intended answer.

Exercise

Return the sorted intersection of two sorted ID lists: [1, 2, 4, 5, 8] and [2, 3, 5, 8, 9] → [2, 5, 8]. Use O(1) extra space besides the output.

Show solution

This is an inner join of two sorted key lists, O(n + m).

Valid Palindrome

In plain words

One pointer at each end walks inwards. Skip anything that is not a letter or digit, compare the rest ignoring case.

The problem

A phrase is a palindrome if, after lowercasing and removing all non-alphanumeric characters, it reads the same forwards and backwards. Given a string s, return True if it is a palindrome.

Inputs = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"
OutputTrue
"amanaplanacanalpanama"

Inputs = " "
OutputTrue
Empty after cleaning.

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Which characters count?Letters and digits only, case-insensitive.
Empty string?True.
Can I use extra memory?Yes, but I'll show an O(1) version too.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 4 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Simple version: build a cleaned, lowercased string and compare it with its reverse. O(n) time, O(n) space. Perfectly fine to say first.

Hint 2

Interviewer follow-up: "without extra memory?" Put one pointer at each end. Skip characters that are not alphanumeric. Compare the two characters case-insensitively. If they differ, it is not a palindrome. Move both inwards. Stop when they meet.

Hint 3

Why two pointers fit: a palindrome is defined by comparing position i from the start with position i from the end. Two pointers walking inwards do exactly that, with no copy.

Hint 4

Bug to avoid: the inner skip loops must also check left < right, or a string full of punctuation runs off the end.

Two Sum II (Sorted Input)

LeetCode 167MediumTwo pointers on sorted data★ Core 40Optimal O(n)
In plain words

Sorted input: too small → move left up; too big → move right down. Each move safely throws away one number.

The problem

Given a sorted (ascending) list numbers and a target, return the 1-based indices [i, j] of the two numbers that add up to target. Use only O(1) extra space.

Inputnumbers = [2, 7, 11, 15], target = 9
Output[1, 2]
Inputnumbers = [-1, 0], target = -1
Output[1, 2]

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Exactly one solution?Yes.
1-based indices?Yes, as LeetCode asks.
Why not the hash map from Two Sum?It works but uses O(n) space; this asks for O(1).
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 3 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

The sorted order is the hint. Put left at the smallest number and right at the largest.

Hint 2
  • If numbers[left] + numbers[right] is too small, the only way to increase the sum is to move left right (to a bigger number). Moving right left would only make it smaller.
  • If the sum is too big, move right left.
  • If it equals the target, return.
Hint 3

Why this never misses the answer: when the sum is too small, numbers[left] cannot pair with anything, because even the biggest remaining number was not enough. So discarding it is safe. The same argument works for right when the sum is too big. Being able to explain this "safe to discard" argument is what makes the answer convincing.

Two Pointers · Coding question

3Sum

LeetCode 15MediumSort + fix one + two pointers★ Core 40Optimal O(n²)
In plain words

Sort. Fix nums[i], then find two numbers after it that sum to −nums[i] with two pointers. Skip repeats to avoid duplicate triplets.

The problem

Given nums, return all unique triplets [a, b, c] with a + b + c == 0. The answer must not contain duplicate triplets.

Inputnums = [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4]
Output[[-1, -1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]
Inputnums = [0, 0, 0]
Output[[0, 0, 0]]

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Unique by value, not by index?Yes. [-1, 0, 1] appears once even if there are two -1s.
Order of output?Any order.
Size?Up to 3000, so O(n²) is fine, O(n³) is not.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 5 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Brute force: three nested loops, O(n³), plus a set of sorted tuples to remove duplicate triplets.

Hint 2

Reduce to a problem you already know. Fix the first number a = nums[i]. Now you need two numbers in the rest that sum to -a. That is Two Sum. If the array is sorted, it is Two Sum II, solvable with two pointers in O(n). Doing that for each i gives O(n²).

Hint 3

Handling duplicates is the real difficulty: 1. Sort first. Equal values become neighbours. 2. Skip i if nums[i] == nums[i-1], since that first value was already fully explored. 3. After finding a triplet, move both pointers and skip over repeated values on both sides.

Hint 4

Early stop: once nums[i] > 0, every remaining number is positive, so no sum can reach 0.

Hint 5

Interview meta-lesson: "k-Sum" problems reduce to "fix one, solve (k−1)-Sum". Say that sentence.

Two Pointers · Coding question

Container With Most Water

LeetCode 11MediumTwo pointers, move the shorter sideOptimal O(n)
In plain words

Water is limited by the shorter line. Moving the taller line can only lose width, so always move the shorter one.

The problem

height[i] is the height of a vertical line at position i. Pick two lines that, together with the x-axis, hold the most water. Return that amount. Area = min(height[i], height[j]) * (j - i).

Inputheight = [1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7]
Output49
Lines at index 1 (8) and 8 (7): min(8, 7) × 7 = 49.

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
At least two lines?Yes.
Heights non-negative?Yes.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 5 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Brute force: check every pair, O(n²).

Hint 2

Start wide. Pointers at both ends give the maximum width. Every move inward reduces width by 1, so a move only helps if the height limit goes up.

Hint 3

Which pointer to move? The area is limited by the shorter line. If you move the taller line inward, the width shrinks and the limit is still at most the shorter line, so the area can only get worse. Moving the shorter line is the only move that could find a taller limit.

Hint 4

Why it is safe: the shorter line at its current position has already been paired with the widest possible partner. Any other partner is closer, so the shorter line can never do better. You can discard it.

Hint 5

This "discard the side that can no longer win" argument is the same as in Two Sum II. Interviewers want to hear it.

Move Zeroes

LeetCode 283EasySlow/fast pointers, in placeOptimal O(n)
In plain words

slow is where the next non-zero belongs. fast reads every element. Non-zeros are swapped forward.

The problem

Move all 0s in nums to the end in place, keeping the relative order of the non-zero elements.

Inputnums = [0, 1, 0, 3, 12]
Output[1, 3, 12, 0, 0]

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
In place?Yes, no copy of the list.
Keep order of non-zeros?Yes (a stable partition).
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 4 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Easy but not in place: build a list of non-zeros and pad with zeros. O(n) time, O(n) space.

Hint 2

In place with two pointers: slow marks where the next non-zero should go; fast scans every element. When fast finds a non-zero, swap it into position slow and advance slow. Everything before slow is the non-zeros in original order; everything from slow to fast is zeros.

Hint 3

Why swap instead of overwrite? Swapping moves the zero to fast's position, so you finish in one pass without a second "fill with zeros" loop.

Hint 4

This slow/fast "write pointer and read pointer" idea solves a whole family: remove duplicates from a sorted array, remove a value, partition by condition.

In plain words

The empty space is at the end of nums1, so write the larger of the two tails into the last free slot.

The problem

nums1 has length m + n: the first m items are sorted values and the last n are zeros (empty space). nums2 has n sorted values. Merge nums2 into nums1 in place so nums1 is sorted.

Inputnums1 = [1, 2, 3, 0, 0, 0], m = 3, nums2 = [2, 5, 6], n = 3

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
In place in nums1?Yes.
Can n be 0?Yes, then nothing changes.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 4 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Simple: copy nums2 into the empty slots and sort. O((m+n) log(m+n)). Works, but ignores that both inputs are sorted.

Hint 2

Merging from the front overwrites values in nums1 you have not used yet.

Hint 3

The trick: merge from the back. The empty space is at the end, so fill nums1 from the last index backwards with the larger of the two current tails. You never overwrite an unread value, because the write position is always at or beyond the read position in nums1.

Hint 4

Stopping: when nums2 is exhausted, the remaining nums1 values are already in place. If nums1 runs out first, copy what is left of nums2.

Hints 3 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Counting sort, two passes: count the 0s, 1s and 2s, then overwrite. O(n), simple and correct.

Hint 2

One pass with three regions: keep low (everything before it is 0), high (everything after it is 2), and mid scanning. - nums[mid] == 0 → swap with low, move both low and mid forward. - nums[mid] == 1 → it is already in the middle region; move mid. - nums[mid] == 2 → swap with high, move high back, but do not move mid: the value swapped in from high has not been examined yet.

Hint 3

That last rule is where everyone slips; say it out loud.

Two Pointers · Coding question

Trapping Rain Water

LeetCode 42HardTwo pointers with running maxesOptimal O(n)
In plain words

If the left max is lower than the right side, the water above the left bar is decided by the left max alone.

The problem

Given bar heights, compute how much rain water is trapped between the bars after raining.

Inputheight = [0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 2, 1]
Output6

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Width of each bar?1.
Non-negative heights?Yes.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 4 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Water above one bar = min(highest bar to its left, highest bar to its right) − its own height, if positive. The water level is set by the lower of the two walls.

Hint 2

Brute force: for each bar, scan left and right for the maxima: O(n²).

Hint 3

Precompute: arrays left_max[i] and right_max[i] in two passes, then one more pass sums the water: O(n) time, O(n) space.

Hint 4

Two pointers, O(1) space: move inward from both ends, tracking left_max and right_max. If left_max < right_max, the left bar's water is fully decided by left_max (some wall on the right is at least as tall), so add left_max − height[left] and move left. Otherwise do the same on the right. Each step settles one bar.

Sliding Window

Keep a running summary of a contiguous range, and update it as the range slides, instead of recomputing from scratch each time.

▭
Think of it like this

A train window passing scenery. You never re-look at the whole landscape: as the train moves, one tree enters on the right and one leaves on the left. You only update what changed.

Any question about a contiguous stretch (substring, subarray, last k days) can keep a running summary of the current stretch. Moving the stretch by one only needs one add and one remove, instead of recomputing everything.

Watch the pattern

Spot it in a question

contiguous subarray / substringlongest / shortest such thatat most krolling / moving averagelast k elements

The template

Common mistakes

  • Using a window when numbers can be negative (use prefix sums instead).
  • Moving left backwards.
  • Recording the answer before the window is valid again.

Practise this pattern (9 questions)

EBest Time to Buy and Sell StockMLongest Substring Without Repeating CharactersEMaximum Average Subarray IMMinimum Size Subarray SumMLongest Repeating Character ReplacementMPermutation in StringHMinimum Window SubstringMFind All Anagrams in a StringHSliding Window Maximum
Concept video in Telugu SRK Codes channel ↗
▶Sliding Window Technique | Real-Life Example, Types, Use CasesSRK Codes · Telugu · Python

Deeper notes

Signals that a window fits

The problem mentions a contiguous subarray or substring, and words like "longest", "shortest", "maximum sum", "at most k", "every k elements" or "rolling".

Fixed-size window: moving average

Add the element entering the window, subtract the element leaving it. Each step is O(1).

Recomputing sum(nums[i:i+k]) each time is O(n·k). The window is O(n).

Variable-size window: grow right, shrink left

Longest substring without repeating characters (LeetCode 3). Expand right one step at a time; when the window breaks the rule, move left forward until it is valid again.

The general template

Connect the dots

A fixed window is SQL's AVG(x) OVER (ORDER BY dt ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), a 7-day rolling average. A variable window answers "alert if more than 100 errors arrive within any 60 seconds", a classic streaming question for Kinesis or Flink.

Exercise

Given sorted event timestamps in seconds, return the maximum number of events inside any 60-second window. [1, 10, 50, 61, 62, 130] → 4 (events at 10, 50, 61, 62 all fit in 10..70).

Show solution

Each pointer moves forward at most n times, so it is O(n) even with the inner while.

Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock

LeetCode 121EasyRunning minimum (one-pass window)★ Core 40Optimal O(n)
In plain words

If you sell today, the best day to have bought is the cheapest day before it. One pass, one variable.

The problem

prices[i] is a stock's price on day i. Choose one day to buy and a later day to sell. Return the maximum profit, or 0 if no profit is possible.

Inputprices = [7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]
Output5
Buy at 1 (day 1), sell at 6 (day 4).
Inputprices = [7, 6, 4, 3, 1]
Output0
Prices only fall.

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Must sell after buying?Yes, sell day > buy day.
One transaction only?Yes.
Empty list?Return 0.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 5 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Brute force: every pair (buy day, later sell day), O(n²).

Hint 2

Flip the viewpoint to the sell day. If I sell today, the best I could have done is buy at the lowest price seen before today. So I only need one number from the past: the running minimum.

Hint 3

One pass: keep min_price so far. For each price, profit if sold today is price - min_price. Track the best. Then update min_price.

Hint 4

Why this is a window: the left edge of the window is the cheapest day so far; the right edge is today. The left edge jumps forward whenever a new minimum appears.

Hint 5

General lesson: when a pair problem has "earlier element vs later element", sweep left to right and keep the best earlier element in a variable.

Sliding Window · Coding question

Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters

LeetCode 3MediumVariable sliding window + last-seen map★ Core 40Optimal O(n)
In plain words

The window never contains a repeat. When a repeat enters, jump the left edge just past its previous position.

The problem

Given a string s, return the length of the longest substring (contiguous) with no repeated characters.

Inputs = "abcabcbb"
Output3
"abc"
Inputs = "bbbbb"
Output1
Inputs = "pwwkew"
Output3
"wke". Note "pwke" is not contiguous.

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Substring means contiguous?Yes.
Character set?Any characters, including spaces.
Empty string?Return 0.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 5 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Brute force: check every substring for uniqueness. O(n³), or O(n²) if you extend each start with a set until a repeat.

Hint 2

Window idea. Keep a window [left, right] that is always valid (no repeats). Extend right one character at a time. If the new character is already in the window, the window must shrink from the left until that earlier copy is gone.

Hint 3

Shrink fast: instead of moving left one step at a time, remember the last index of each character. When you see ch again and its last index is inside the window, jump left to last[ch] + 1 in one step.

Hint 4

The subtle check: last[ch] >= left. A character might have been seen long ago, before the current window started. That old sighting must not move left backwards.

Hint 5

Recognise the pattern: "longest contiguous ... such that [constraint]" means variable window: grow right, shrink left while invalid, record the best.

I check last[ch] >= left so an old sighting outside the window doesn't move left backwards. Each step is O(1), so O(n) time and O(k) space for the map."

Follow-up questions they ask next

At most k distinct characters (LeetCode 340)?

Window with a Counter; while len(counter) > k, decrement s[left] and delete it at zero, then move left.

Connect it to your AWS work

"Longest stretch without a repeat" maps to longest run of unique events per session or detecting when a device ID first repeats in a stream. The window-with-a-map shape is the standard streaming pattern for Kinesis or Flink consumers.

Remember it in one line

Grow right; if ch was last seen inside the window, jump left to last[ch] + 1.

Sliding Window · Coding question

Maximum Average Subarray I

LeetCode 643EasyFixed-size sliding windowOptimal O(n)
In plain words

Neighbouring windows share k − 1 numbers. Update the sum with the one entering and the one leaving.

The problem

Given nums and an integer k, find the contiguous subarray of length exactly k with the maximum average, and return that average.

Inputnums = [1, 12, -5, -6, 50, 3], k = 4
Output12.75
(12 − 5 − 6 + 50) / 4

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
k ≤ len(nums)?Yes.
Return type?A float.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 4 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Brute force: compute sum(nums[i:i+k]) for every start. That is O(n·k).

Hint 2

The waste: neighbouring windows share k−1 elements. Moving the window one step right only adds one element on the right and removes one on the left.

Hint 3

So keep a running sum: compute the first window once, then for each step window += nums[i] - nums[i-k]. Each step is O(1), so the whole thing is O(n).

Hint 4

Small trick: maximise the sum, not the average, and divide once at the end. Dividing every step is wasted work.

Sliding Window · Coding question

Minimum Size Subarray Sum

LeetCode 209MediumVariable window, shrink while valid★ Core 40Optimal O(n)
In plain words

Positive numbers only: adding raises the sum, removing lowers it. Shrink from the left as long as the sum stays ≥ target.

The problem

Given an array of positive integers nums and a target, return the minimal length of a contiguous subarray whose sum is at least target, or 0 if none exists.

Inputtarget = 7, nums = [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3]
Output2
[4, 3]
Inputtarget = 11, nums = [1, 1, 1, 1]
Output0

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
All positive?Yes. This is what makes the window valid.
At least or exactly?At least target.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 4 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Brute force: every start, extend until the sum reaches target, record the length. O(n²).

Hint 2

Why a window works here: all numbers are positive, so adding an element always increases the sum and removing one always decreases it. That monotonic behaviour is the condition for a sliding window.

Hint 3

This is the "shortest" flavour of the window template: 1. Extend right, add nums[right]. 2. While the window is valid (sum ≥ target), record its length, then remove nums[left] and move left forward to try a shorter window.

Hint 4

Compare with "longest" problems, where you shrink while the window is invalid and record after. Knowing which of the two flavours you need is half the battle.

Sliding Window · Coding question

Longest Repeating Character Replacement

LeetCode 424MediumWindow + counts: window − maxfreq ≤ kOptimal O(n)
In plain words

A window is fine if (length − count of its most common letter) ≤ k. Otherwise slide the left edge by one.

The problem

Given an uppercase string s and an integer k, you may change at most k characters to any other uppercase letter. Return the length of the longest substring containing a single repeated letter after the changes.

Inputs = "ABAB", k = 2
Output4
Change both A's to B (or vice versa).
Inputs = "AABABBA", k = 1
Output4
"AABA" → "AAAA".

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Uppercase letters only?Yes.
Must I use all k changes?No, at most k.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 4 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Key question for any window: what makes a window valid?

Hint 2

A window can be turned into one repeated letter if we keep its most frequent letter and change everything else. The number of changes needed is window_length - max_count. The window is valid when that is ≤ k.

Hint 3

Algorithm: grow right, update the count of the new letter and max_count. If window_length - max_count > k, shrink from the left by one (decrement that letter's count).

Hint 4

The famous subtlety: you do not need to decrease max_count when shrinking. A stale, too-high max_count can only make us keep a window the same size, never record a bigger wrong answer, because the answer only grows when a genuinely higher max_count appears. Explaining this earns credit; if unsure, recomputing max(counts.values()) (26 letters) is still O(26·n) = O(n).

Permutation in String

LeetCode 567MediumFixed window + count comparisonOptimal O(26·n) = O(n)
In plain words

A permutation has the same letter counts. Slide a window the size of s1 over s2 and compare counts.

The problem

Given strings s1 and s2, return True if s2 contains a permutation of s1 as a contiguous substring.

Inputs1 = "ab", s2 = "eidbaooo"
OutputTrue
"ba" is a permutation of "ab".
Inputs1 = "ab", s2 = "eidboaoo"

Clarify before you code

AskAssume
Lowercase letters only?Yes.
s1 longer than s2?Then False.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 4 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

A permutation of s1 is any string with the same letter counts. So the question is: does any window of length len(s1) in s2 have the same counts as s1?

Hint 2

Brute force: for every window, build a Counter and compare. O(n · m).

Hint 3

Sliding the window: the window length is fixed, so when it moves one step, one letter enters and one leaves. Update the window's counts in O(1) and compare the two count tables. With 26 letters, comparing is O(26), so the total is O(26·n) = O(n).

Hint 4

Even faster comparison: keep a matches counter of how many of the 26 letters currently have equal counts and update it as letters enter and leave. Mention it as an optimisation; the Counter-compare version is perfectly acceptable.

Minimum Window Substring

LeetCode 76HardVariable window + 'have vs need' counterOptimal O(|s| + |t|)
In plain words

Grow right until every needed letter is covered. Then shrink left while it stays covered, recording the smallest.

The problem

Given strings s and t, return the smallest substring of s that contains every character of t (including duplicates). Return "" if none exists.

Inputs = "ADOBECODEBANC", t = "ABC"
Output"BANC"
Inputs = "a", t = "aa"
Output""

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Duplicates in t count?Yes: t = "aa" needs two a's.
Case-sensitive?Yes.
Unique answer?Yes.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 5 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

This is the hardest common window problem, but it is the same "shortest valid window" template as Minimum Size Subarray Sum, with a smarter validity check.

Hint 2

Valid window: every character of t appears in the window at least as many times as in t.

Hint 3

Checking validity in O(1): keep need = Counter(t) and a window Counter. Keep formed = how many distinct characters currently meet their required count. The window is valid when formed == len(need). - When a character enters and its window count reaches exactly need[ch], formed += 1. - When a character leaves and its window count drops below need[ch], formed -= 1.

Hint 4

Loop: extend right; while valid, record the window if it is the smallest so far, then drop s[left] and move left.

Hint 5

If you get stuck in an interview: write the brute force, then say "the validity check is the bottleneck, so I track how many required characters are satisfied". That sentence alone shows the right idea.

Sliding Window · Coding question

Sliding Window Maximum

LeetCode 239HardMonotonic dequeOptimal O(n)
In plain words

A new value pops every smaller value from the back (they can never win again). The front leaves when it slides out.

The problem

Return the maximum of every contiguous window of size k as the window slides from left to right.

Inputnums = [1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7], k = 3
Output[3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
k ≤ len(nums)?Yes.
Size?Up to 10⁵, so O(n·k) is too slow.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 4 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Brute force: max(nums[i:i+k]) for every window: O(n·k).

Hint 2

Heap: push (−value, index); pop the top while its index is outside the window. O(n log n).

Hint 3

Monotonic deque, O(n): keep indexes in a deque whose values are decreasing from front to back. - When a new value arrives, pop smaller values from the back: they can never be a maximum again while this bigger, newer value is in the window. - Pop the front if it has slid out of the window. - The front is always the current maximum.

Hint 4

Each index is added and removed once, so the total is O(n). The "useless elements get removed" argument is what the interviewer wants to hear.

Stacks & Queues

A stack is last-in-first-out (a pile of plates). A queue is first-in-first-out (a line at a counter).

☰
Think of it like this

A stack is a pile of plates: you take the last one you put down. A queue is a ticket counter line: first come, first served. Choosing the right one is about which item you need next.

Nested things (brackets, JSON, function calls) close in reverse order of opening, so a stack fits. "Next greater" questions also use a stack: items wait on it until something bigger arrives and resolves them.

Watch the pattern

Spot it in a question

brackets / nestedmost recent firstundonext greater / smallerevaluate expressionBFS order (queue)

The template

Common mistakes

  • list.pop(0) for a queue (O(n)); use deque.popleft().
  • Popping from an empty stack.
  • Forgetting leftovers on the stack at the end.

Deeper notes

In Python

Classic: valid brackets

Push every opening bracket. On a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its matching opener.

Monotonic stack: "next greater element"

For each day, how many days until a warmer temperature? Keep a stack of indexes whose answer is still unknown. When a warmer day arrives, it resolves everything colder on the stack.

Each index is pushed and popped once, so O(n) despite the nested loop.

Connect the dots

A queue is how SQS hands work to consumers and how BFS explores a graph level by level. A stack is how a parser checks nested JSON or SQL brackets, and how DFS works without recursion. The monotonic stack answers "next time the price or row count went above today's value".

In plain words

The bracket you close must be the most recently opened one. Last in, first out: a stack.

The problem

Given a string of ()[]{} characters, return True if every opening bracket is closed by the same type of bracket in the correct order.

Inputs = "()[]{}"
OutputTrue
Inputs = "(]"
OutputFalse
Inputs = "([)]"
OutputFalse
Closed in the wrong order.
Inputs = "{[]}"
OutputTrue

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Only bracket characters?Yes. If other characters appear, ignore them.
Empty string?True.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 4 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

What makes nesting valid? The bracket closed now must be the most recently opened one that is still open. "Most recent first" is exactly last-in-first-out, which is a stack.

Hint 2

Algorithm: push every opening bracket. On a closing bracket, the stack must be non-empty and its top must be the matching opener; pop it. At the end, the stack must be empty (nothing left unclosed).

Hint 3

A naive idea that fails: counting opens and closes per type. "([)]" has balanced counts but invalid order. Mention this; it shows you understand why the stack is needed.

Hint 4

Clean code tip: a dict mapping each closer to its opener avoids a chain of if/elif.

Say it like this

"The most recently opened bracket must close first, which is last-in-first-out, so a stack fits. I push openers; for a closer, I check the stack isn't empty and the popped opener matches, using a dict from closer to opener. At the end the stack must be empty. O(n) time and space. Simple counting wouldn't work because ([)] has balanced counts but bad order."

Follow-up questions they ask next

Minimum additions to make it valid (LeetCode 921)?

Track open_needed: on ( increment balance; on ) decrement if positive, else count an insertion. Answer = insertions + remaining balance.

Longest valid parentheses (LeetCode 32, hard)?

Stack of indexes, seeded with -1; length = i − stack top after each pop.

Connect it to your AWS work

Bracket matching is how a parser validates JSON payloads and SQL expressions. If you ever wrote a pre-check for malformed JSON lines before a Glue job, this is the core of it.

Remember it in one line

Last opened, first closed → stack. Closer must match the popped opener; stack empty at the end.

Min Stack

LeetCode 155MediumStack that stores the min alongside each valueOptimal O(1) every operation
In plain words

Store (value, min so far). The top entry always knows the current minimum, and popping restores the old one.

The problem

Design a stack with push(x), pop(), top() and get_min(), where every operation runs in O(1).

Inputpush(-2), push(0), push(-3), get_min(), pop(), top(), get_min()
Output-3, 0, -2

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Will pop/top/get_min be called on an empty stack?No, assume valid calls.
Duplicates allowed?Yes.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 5 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Naive: keep a normal list and compute min(stack) on demand: O(n) per get_min.

Hint 2

Keep one variable for the minimum? Fails on pop: if you pop the current minimum, you do not know the previous minimum.

Hint 3

Key insight: the minimum depends only on what is below. Store, for each element, the minimum of the stack at the time it was pushed. Then the top entry always knows the current minimum, and popping automatically restores the previous one.

Hint 4

Implementation: push tuples (value, min_so_far), or keep a second stack of minimums. Both are O(1) per operation and O(n) space.

Hint 5

Design questions like this test whether you think about state that must survive undo operations.

Test it yourself

Paste a solution into a .py file and run these checks. Every solution here has been run against them.

Say it like this

"Computing min on demand is O(n). A single min variable breaks on pop. Since the minimum at any level depends only on what's below it, I'll store each value together with the minimum at the time it was pushed. The top always holds the current min, and popping restores the previous one automatically. Every operation is O(1), with O(n) space."

Follow-up questions they ask next

Reduce space?

Use a second stack that only pushes when x <= current min, and pops when the popped value equals its top. Same O(1) time, less space when values are mostly larger than the min.

Max stack, or min queue?

Max stack: same idea with max. Min queue: two min-stacks (in-stack and out-stack), amortised O(1).

Connect it to your AWS work

Storing an aggregate alongside each version so you can roll back cheaply is how snapshot-based table formats work: each Iceberg snapshot carries its own summary stats, so going back a snapshot does not require recomputation.

Remember it in one line

Push (value, min so far). The top always knows the current min.

Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation

LeetCode 150MediumStack of operandsOptimal O(n)
In plain words

In Reverse Polish Notation an operator uses the two most recent numbers. Pop the right operand first.

The problem

Evaluate an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation (operators come after their operands). Tokens are integers or + - * /. Division truncates toward zero.

Inputtokens = ["2", "1", "+", "3", "*"]
Output9
(2 + 1) * 3
Inputtokens = ["4", "13", "5", "/", "+"]
Output6
4 + (13 / 5) = 4 + 2

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Always a valid expression?Yes.
Division rounding?Toward zero: −7 / 2 = −3, not −4.
Negative numbers as tokens?Yes, like "-11".
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 4 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

In RPN, an operator applies to the two most recent values. "Most recent" again means a stack.

Hint 2

Algorithm: for each token, if it is a number, push it. If it is an operator, pop b (the right operand) then a (the left operand), compute a op b, push the result. At the end, the single value on the stack is the answer.

Hint 3

Two classic bugs: 1. Operand order. The first pop is the right operand. a - b, not b - a. 2. Division. Python's // floors (−7 // 2 = −4). The problem wants truncation toward zero, so use int(a / b).

Hint 4

Detecting numbers: "-11" is a number, so do not test token[0] == "-"; test whether the token is one of the four operators instead.

Stack · Coding question

Daily Temperatures

LeetCode 739MediumMonotonic decreasing stack★ Core 40Optimal O(n)
In plain words

Keep days that are still waiting for warmer weather. A warmer day pops every colder waiting day and answers it.

The problem

Given daily temperatures, return a list where answer[i] is the number of days you have to wait after day i for a warmer temperature, or 0 if none comes.

Inputtemperatures = [73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73]
Output[1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0]

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Strictly warmer?Yes.
Size?Up to 10⁵, so O(n²) is too slow.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 5 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Brute force: for each day, scan forward until a warmer day. O(n²) on a falling sequence.

Hint 2

Flip it around: let the warm day resolve the waiting days. Keep a stack of days that are still waiting for a warmer day. When today is warmer than the day on top of the stack, today is that day's answer: pop it and record today - that_day. Keep popping while today beats the top. Then push today, since it is now waiting too.

Hint 3

Why the stack stays decreasing: anything colder than today gets popped before today is pushed. So the stack always holds temperatures in decreasing order from bottom to top. That is a monotonic stack.

Hint 4

Why it is O(n): each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the nested while loop does O(n) work in total.

Hint 5

Pattern trigger: "next greater", "next smaller", "previous greater", "days until". All are monotonic stacks.

Stack · Coding question

Decode String

LeetCode 394MediumStack of (previous string, repeat count)Optimal O(output length)
In plain words

On '[' push (text so far, repeat count) and start fresh. On ']' pop and attach the repeated inner text.

The problem

Decode a string encoded as k[encoded], meaning encoded repeated k times. Encodings can be nested.

Inputs = "3[a]2[bc]"
Output"aaabcbc"
Inputs = "3[a2[c]]"
Output"accaccacc"
Inputs = "2[abc]3[cd]ef"
Output"abcabccdcdcdef"

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Always valid?Yes.
Can k have several digits?Yes, like 12[a].
Digits only appear as counts?Yes.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 3 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Nesting means you must pause the outer work, finish the inner part, then resume. Pausing and resuming in reverse order is a stack (or recursion, which uses the call stack).

Hint 2

Track two things while scanning: current (the string built at this level) and num (the repeat count being read). - Digit: num = num * 10 + digit (handles multi-digit counts). - [: entering a deeper level. Push (current, num) to save the outer state, then reset both. - ]: leaving the level. Pop (prev, k) and set current = prev + current * k. - Letter: append to current.

Hint 3

Why push the previous string, not just the count? Because after the inner part is repeated, it must be attached to whatever was built before the [.

Say it like this

On [ I push the pair (current, num) and reset; on ] I pop and set current = prev + current * k. Time and space are proportional to the output length. A recursive parser works too, but the explicit stack avoids recursion limits."

Binary Search

On sorted data, check the middle and throw away half each time. A million items take about 20 steps.

½
Think of it like this

Guessing a number between 1 and 1,000 when told "higher" or "lower". Always guess the middle and you need at most 10 guesses. Each answer throws away half of what is left.

Whenever data is sorted, or the answer has a yes/no test that flips once (too slow… too slow… fast enough), you can halve the search space each step: O(log n).

Watch the pattern

Spot it in a question

sortedfind position / first / lastminimum X such that…maximum X such that…rotated sorted array

The template

Common mistakes

  • Mixing while lo <= hi with hi = mid (infinite loop).
  • Off-by-one when returning lo vs lo − 1.
  • Forgetting binary search works on answers, not only on arrays.

Deeper notes

The basic version

First occurrence (lower bound)

With duplicates, interviewers usually want the first position. Keep searching left even after a match.

Binary search on the answer

The most useful variant for senior rounds. If you can write can_do(x) that is false for small x and true for large x, binary-search the smallest x that works.

Example: packages with these weights must ship in order within days days. What is the smallest truck capacity that works?

Connect the dots

Ship-within-days is a capacity-planning question in disguise: "what is the smallest batch size (or number of DPUs) that finishes all files inside the SLA?". Plain binary search is how Parquet and Iceberg use sorted min/max statistics to skip files and row groups, and how you locate a timestamp inside sorted data.

Off-by-one checklist

Decide if hi is inclusive or exclusive, and stay consistent: while lo <= hi with hi = mid - 1, or while lo < hi with hi = mid. Mixing them causes infinite loops.

Exercise

Given sorted hourly file start times [0, 60, 120, 180] (minutes), return which file contains minute 135 (the last file whose start ≤ 135). Expected: index 2.

Binary Search · Coding question

Binary Search

LeetCode 704EasyClassic binary searchOptimal O(log n)
In plain words

Look at the middle. If it is too small, the answer can only be on the right; if too big, only on the left.

The problem

Given a sorted list of distinct integers nums and a target, return its index, or -1 if it is not present. Must be O(log n).

Inputnums = [-1, 0, 3, 5, 9, 12], target = 9
Output4
Inputnums = [-1, 0, 3, 5, 9, 12], target = 2
Output-1

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Sorted ascending, distinct?Yes.
Empty list?Return -1.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 4 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Linear scan is O(n) and ignores the sorting.

Hint 2

Binary search halves the search space each step. Look at the middle element: - equal → found; - middle smaller than target → the target can only be to the right, so discard the left half; - middle bigger → discard the right half.

Hint 3

The invariant to say out loud: "if the target exists, it is always inside [lo, hi]." Every update must keep that true. With hi inclusive, the loop runs while lo <= hi, and the updates are lo = mid + 1 / hi = mid - 1 (mid is already ruled out).

Hint 4

Overflow note: in Java/C++ people write lo + (hi - lo) // 2 to avoid integer overflow. Python ints do not overflow, but mentioning it shows breadth.

Inputnums = [5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10], target = 8

Inputnums = [5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10], target = 6
Output[-1, -1]

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Duplicates?Yes, that is the point.
Empty list?[-1, -1].
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 5 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Tempting but wrong: binary search to find any 8, then walk left and right. If all n elements equal the target, the walk is O(n).

Hint 2

Better: two binary searches. - Lower bound: the first index where nums[i] >= target. - Upper bound: the first index where nums[i] > target. The last occurrence is that minus 1.

Hint 3

The lower-bound template (half-open [lo, hi)): lo, hi = 0, len(nums); while lo < hi: if nums[mid] < target then lo = mid + 1 else hi = mid. When the loop ends, lo is the answer.

Hint 4

The difference from classic search: on a match you keep searching left (hi = mid) instead of returning. Memorise this template; it solves a whole family of "first index where condition becomes true" problems.

Hint 5

Python shortcut: bisect_left is lower bound and bisect_right is upper bound. Use them if allowed, but be ready to write them.

Binary Search · Coding question

Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array

LeetCode 153MediumBinary search on a rotated arrayOptimal O(log n)
In plain words

A rotated array is a high run then a low run. If mid > right end, mid is in the high run, so the minimum is to the right.

The problem

A sorted array of distinct values was rotated at an unknown pivot (e.g. [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] → [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]). Return the minimum element in O(log n).

Inputnums = [3, 4, 5, 1, 2]
Output1
Inputnums = [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]
Output0
Inputnums = [11, 13, 15, 17]
Output11
Not rotated (or rotated n times).

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Distinct values?Yes. Duplicates make the worst case O(n) (LeetCode 154).
Could it be unrotated?Yes.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 4 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Picture the array as two sorted runs: a high run then a low run, like [4, 5, 6, 7 | 0, 1, 2]. The minimum is the first element of the low run.

Hint 2

Compare the middle with the right end: - If nums[mid] > nums[hi], mid is in the high run, so the minimum is strictly to the right: lo = mid + 1. - Otherwise mid is in the low run (or the array is not rotated), so the minimum is at mid or to its left: hi = mid.

Hint 3

Why compare with the right end, not the left? Comparing with nums[hi] works for the unrotated case too. Comparing with the left end makes the unrotated case ambiguous. If you get confused in the interview, draw the two runs; the picture answers it.

Hint 4

Loop ends when lo == hi, which is the index of the minimum.

Binary Search · Coding question

Search in Rotated Sorted Array

LeetCode 33MediumBinary search: find the sorted halfOptimal O(log n)
In plain words

At every mid, one side is in order. Check whether the target fits inside that side's range; if not, go the other way.

The problem

Given a rotated sorted array of distinct integers and a target, return the target's index or -1, in O(log n).

Inputnums = [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], target = 0
Output4
Inputnums = [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], target = 3
Output-1

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Distinct values?Yes.
O(log n) required?Yes.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 4 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Option 1 (two steps): find the rotation point with Find Minimum, then run ordinary binary search on the correct half. Clean and easy to explain.

Hint 2

Option 2 (one pass): at any mid, at least one half is sorted. Work out which one: - If nums[lo] <= nums[mid], the left half [lo..mid] is sorted. If the target lies within nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid], search left; otherwise search right. - Otherwise the right half [mid..hi] is sorted. If nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi], search right; otherwise search left.

Hint 3

Why it works: in a sorted half you can tell for certain whether the target is inside by checking its two ends. If it is not inside, it must be in the other half.

Hint 4

Interview advice: if the one-pass conditions feel shaky, present the two-step version. A correct, clear answer beats a buggy clever one.

Binary Search · Coding question

Koko Eating Bananas

LeetCode 875MediumBinary search on the answer★ Core 40Optimal O(n · log max(piles))
In plain words

If speed k is fast enough, every faster speed is too. So search the speed range for the first speed that works.

The problem

There are piles of bananas and h hours. Each hour Koko picks one pile and eats up to k bananas from it (if the pile has fewer, she finishes it and waits). Return the minimum integer speed k that lets her finish within h hours.

Inputpiles = [3, 6, 7, 11], h = 8
Output4
Inputpiles = [30, 11, 23, 4, 20], h = 5
Output30

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
h ≥ number of piles?Yes, otherwise impossible.
Pile sizes?Up to 10⁹, so trying every speed is too slow.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 6 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

This does not look like binary search, because nothing is sorted. The trick is to search over possible answers.

Hint 2

Step 1: write a feasibility check. For a speed k, hours needed = sum of ceil(pile / k). Feasible if that is ≤ h. This is O(n).

Hint 3

Step 2: notice monotonicity. If speed k works, any faster speed also works. So feasibility looks like F F F F T T T T over k. The answer is the first T, which is exactly a lower-bound binary search.

Hint 4

Step 3: bound the range. The slowest possible useful speed is 1; the fastest you ever need is max(piles) (one pile per hour).

Hint 5

Generic recipe for "minimum X such that ..." problems: write feasible(x), confirm it is monotonic, binary search the smallest feasible x. Same recipe solves ship within D days, split array largest sum, and minimum DPU capacity questions.

Hint 6

Ceil without floats: (p + k - 1) // k or -(-p // k).

Linked Lists

Less common in DE rounds, but three questions show up often enough to learn: reverse, detect a cycle, find the middle.

→
Think of it like this

A treasure hunt: each clue only tells you where the next clue is. You cannot jump to clue 7; you must follow the chain. Changing the route means rewriting where a clue points.

Linked-list questions test careful pointer handling. Three tools solve nearly all of them: a dummy head to avoid special cases, slow/fast pointers to find the middle or a cycle, and the prev/cur/next flip to reverse.

Watch the pattern

Spot it in a question

reversemiddlecyclenth from endmerge sorted lists

The template

Common mistakes

  • Losing the rest of the list by overwriting next before saving it.
  • Comparing node values instead of nodes (is) in cycle checks.
  • Not returning dummy.next.

Practise this pattern (5 questions)

EReverse Linked ListEMerge Two Sorted ListsELinked List CycleMRemove Nth Node From EndEPalindrome Linked List
Concept video in Telugu SRK Codes channel ↗
▶What is a Linked List? | Types & ImplementationSRK Codes · Telugu · Python▶Singly Linked List | Insert, Delete, DisplaySRK Codes · Telugu · Python

Deeper notes

The structure

Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. There is no index; to reach node 5 you walk from the head.

Reverse a linked list

Walk the list and flip each arrow. Keep three references: previous, current, next.

Fast and slow pointers

The fast pointer moves two steps, the slow one moves one. If there is a cycle, fast eventually laps slow. When fast reaches the end, slow is in the middle.

Connect the dots

Iceberg snapshots form a linked chain: each snapshot points to its parent. Walking the chain is how time travel and snapshot expiry work. The same "detect a cycle" idea protects any pointer-following loop, such as following NextToken values from a buggy API.

Exercise

Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted list (LeetCode 21).

Linked List · Coding question

Reverse Linked List

LeetCode 206EasyThree pointers: prev, cur, next★ Core 40Optimal O(n)
In plain words

Keep three references: prev (the reversed part), cur (the node being flipped) and nxt (the rest, saved first).

The problem

Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list and return the new head.

Input1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5
Output5 → 4 → 3 → 2 → 1
Inputempty list
Outputempty list

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
In place?Yes, by re-pointing next, not by creating new nodes.
Empty or single node?Return as is.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 5 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Easy but wasteful: copy values into a Python list, then write them back reversed. O(n) space.

Hint 2

In place: walk the list and turn every arrow around. At each node you need three references: - prev: the already-reversed part (starts as None); - cur: the node you are re-pointing; - nxt: the rest of the list, saved before you overwrite cur.next, or you lose it.

Hint 3

The four lines, in this exact order: save next, flip the arrow, move prev, move cur. At the end prev is the new head.

Hint 4

Draw it. In an interview, sketch three boxes and arrows and step through two iterations. That is how you avoid losing the rest of the list.

Hint 5

Recursive version: reverse the rest, then make head.next.next = head and head.next = None. Elegant, but O(n) stack depth.

Merge Two Sorted Lists

LeetCode 21EasyDummy head + two pointers★ Core 40Optimal O(m + n)
In plain words

A dummy node gives the merged list a fixed starting point. Attach the smaller head each time, then attach the leftovers.

The problem

Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted list by splicing their nodes together. Return the head.

Input1 → 2 → 4 and 1 → 3 → 4
Output1 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 4

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Reuse nodes or create new ones?Reuse (splice).
Either list empty?Return the other one.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 3 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Same as merging two sorted arrays: compare the two heads, take the smaller, advance that list.

Hint 2

The dummy-head trick: without it, you need special code to decide which node becomes the head. Create a placeholder node dummy, keep a tail pointer, always attach to tail.next, and return dummy.next at the end. This trick removes edge cases in almost every linked-list problem that builds a new list.

Hint 3

Leftovers: when one list runs out, attach the rest of the other in one step (tail.next = a or b). No loop needed, since it is already sorted.

Linked List Cycle

LeetCode 141EasyFast and slow pointers (Floyd)Optimal O(n)
In plain words

slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2. With a loop, fast eventually laps slow and they meet. Without one, fast reaches None.

The problem

Return True if the linked list has a cycle, meaning some node's next eventually points back to an earlier node.

Input3 → 2 → 0 → -4 → (back to 2)
OutputTrue
Input1 → 2 → None
OutputFalse

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Can I modify the nodes?No.
Extra memory allowed?Ideally O(1).
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 4 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Hash set approach: walk the list and store each node object (not its value; values can repeat) in a set. If you meet a node already in the set, there is a cycle. O(n) space.

Hint 2

Floyd's tortoise and hare: move slow one step and fast two steps. If there is no cycle, fast reaches the end. If there is a cycle, both pointers eventually go round it, and fast gains one step per move on slow, so it must land on slow.

Hint 3

Why they must meet (the argument interviewers like): once both are inside the cycle, the gap between them shrinks by exactly 1 each step, so it hits 0 and cannot skip over.

Hint 4

Compare nodes with is, not values.

Connect it to your AWS work

Cycle detection protects any pointer-following loop: a pagination API that returns a next_token you have already seen, or a job-dependency chain that loops back. A visited set plus a check is the practical version.

Slow +1, fast +2. Meet → cycle. Fast hits None → no cycle.

Remove Nth Node From End

LeetCode 19MediumTwo pointers with a fixed gapOptimal O(L)
In plain words

Open a gap so that when the front pointer runs off the end, the back pointer sits just before the node to delete.

The problem

Remove the nth node from the end of the list and return the head. Try to do it in one pass.

AskAssume

Hints 3 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Two-pass version: count the length L, then walk to node L − n (the one before the target) and skip the target. Perfectly fine to present first.

Hint 2

One-pass version: put two pointers n + 1 nodes apart, then move both until the front one falls off the end. The back pointer is then exactly one node before the target.

Hint 3

Use a dummy node before the head. If the head itself must be removed, the "node before the target" is the dummy, and the code needs no special case. Return dummy.next.

Heaps & Top-K

A heap always gives you the smallest item in O(1) and adds or removes items in O(log n). It is the tool for "top K", "K-th largest" and "merge K sorted things".

△
Think of it like this

A hospital emergency room: patients do not leave in arrival order, the most urgent one is always seen next. New patients keep arriving and slot into the right place without re-sorting everyone.

When you repeatedly need the smallest or largest item while items keep arriving, a heap gives it in O(log n) per operation instead of re-sorting. Keeping the heap at size k gives top-k in O(n log k).

Watch the pattern

Spot it in a question

top k / k largest / k smallestkth largestmerge k sortedmedian of a streamalways process the cheapest/earliest next

The template

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting heapq is a MIN-heap.
  • Pushing tuples whose second item is not comparable (add an index tie-breaker).
  • Sorting everything when only k items matter.

Practise this pattern (5 questions)

ELast Stone WeightMKth Largest Element in an ArrayMK Closest Points to OriginHMerge k Sorted ListsHFind Median from Data Stream
Concept video in Telugu SRK Codes channel ↗
▶Heaps & Priority Queues | Min vs Max Heap | heapqSRK Codes · Telugu · Python

Deeper notes

heapq basics

Python's heapq is a min-heap stored in a plain list: heap[0] is always the smallest.

Top K frequent

K-th largest with a heap of size K

Keep only the K biggest items seen so far in a min-heap. Its smallest item is the K-th largest. Memory stays O(K) no matter how long the stream is.

Merge K sorted lists

Put the first item of each list in a heap. Repeatedly pop the smallest and push the next item from the same list.

O(N log K) where N is the total number of items and K the number of lists.

Connect the dots

Merge K sorted is external merge sort: to sort 100 GB with 4 GB of RAM, sort 4 GB chunks into separate files, then stream-merge them with a heap holding one line per file. Top-K with a size-K heap is how you answer "top 10 products per day" over a stream without storing everything.

Interview angle

Mention the tie-breaker: when values tie, Python compares the next tuple element. That is why the example pushes (value, i, j) and not the raw object; comparing two dicts would raise TypeError.

Exercise

Given (job_name, runtime_minutes) pairs, return the 3 slowest jobs.

Show solution

Last Stone Weight

LeetCode 1046EasyMax-heap via negationOptimal O(n log n)
In plain words

Python's heapq always gives the smallest. Store −weight, and the smallest stored value is the heaviest stone.

The problem

Each turn, take the two heaviest stones x ≤ y and smash them: if equal both are destroyed, otherwise a stone of weight y − x remains. Return the weight of the last stone, or 0 if none remain.

Inputstones = [2, 7, 4, 1, 8, 1]
Output1
8,7 → 1; 4,2 → 2; 2,1 → 1; 1,1 → 0; left with 1.

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Stones count?Up to 30 in LeetCode, but assume it could be large.
Empty list?Return 0.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 3 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Each turn needs the two largest values, and then inserts a new value. Re-sorting every turn costs O(n log n) per turn, O(n² log n) total.

Hint 2

A heap gives the largest in O(log n) and inserts in O(log n). Python's heapq is a min-heap, so store negated values: the most negative number is the largest stone.

Hint 3

This problem exists to check that you know the negation trick and that you remember to negate back when reading. Mention that heapq has no max-heap and that negation is the standard workaround.

Why not keep a sorted list and use bisect.insort?

Heap / Priority Queue · Coding question

Kth Largest Element in an Array

LeetCode 215MediumMin-heap of size k / quickselect★ Core 40Optimal O(n log k)
In plain words

A min-heap of size k holds the k largest so far. Its smallest member, on top, is the kth largest.

The problem

Return the kth largest element in nums (in sorted order, not the kth distinct). Try to beat O(n log n).

Inputnums = [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], k = 2
Output5
Inputnums = [3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6], k = 4
Output4

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Kth distinct or kth in sorted order?Sorted order; duplicates count.
1 ≤ k ≤ n?Yes.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 4 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Sort and index: sorted(nums)[-k]. O(n log n). Say it first.

Hint 2

Min-heap of size k: keep the k largest values seen so far. Push each number; if the heap grows past k, pop the smallest. At the end, the smallest of the k largest, heap[0], is the answer. O(n log k), O(k) space. This is the version that works on a stream of unknown length, which is why interviewers love it.

Hint 3

Why a MIN-heap for the k LARGEST? Because you want to quickly throw away the weakest member of your top-k club. The weakest member is the smallest, so it must be on top.

Hint 4

Quickselect: partition like quicksort around a pivot, but recurse only into the side that contains position n − k. Average O(n), worst case O(n²) (random pivots make that unlikely). Mention it as the "average linear" answer.

Merge k Sorted Lists

LeetCode 23HardHeap of the current heads★ Core 40Optimal O(N log k)
In plain words

The next smallest value overall is always one of the current heads. Pop it, then push the next node from that same list.

The problem

Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted linked list and return its head.

Input[1→4→5, 1→3→4, 2→6]
Output1→1→2→3→4→4→5→6

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Some lists empty?Yes, and the input list itself may be empty.
Total nodes N, number of lists k?N up to 10⁴, k up to 10⁴.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 5 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Collect and sort: O(N log N). Ignores that each list is already sorted.

Hint 2

Merge one by one: merge list 1 with list 2, then the result with list 3, and so on. The growing result is re-walked each time: O(N · k).

Hint 3

Heap of heads: the next smallest node overall must be the head of one of the k lists. Keep those k heads in a min-heap. Pop the smallest, attach it to the output, and push that list's next node. Each of N nodes is pushed and popped once, and the heap never holds more than k items: O(N log k).

Hint 4

Python detail that bites people: pushing (node.val, node) crashes when two values tie, because Python then tries to compare ListNode objects. Add a unique tie-breaker: (node.val, i, node).

Hint 5

Alternative: divide and conquer, merging lists in pairs (like merge sort): also O(N log k), with no heap.

Say it like this

"The next smallest node must be the head of one of the k lists, so I keep the heads in a min-heap. I pop the smallest, attach it, and push its successor. Each node goes in and out once and the heap holds at most k entries, so O(N log k) time and O(k) space. I push (val, index, node) so ties never compare nodes. Pairwise merging is an equally fast alternative."

Follow-up questions they ask next

Merge k sorted files that do not fit in memory?

Same algorithm with a generator per file: the heap holds one line per file. Python's heapq.merge(*iterators) does exactly this lazily.

Why is one-by-one merging O(N·k)?

The accumulated result is re-walked for each new list, so early nodes are copied up to k times.

Connect it to your AWS work

This is external merge sort and compaction: sort chunks that fit in memory into separate files, then stream-merge them with a heap holding one record per file. heapq.merge gives you that in one line for sorted S3 object streams.

Remember it in one line

Heap of k heads: pop smallest, attach, push its next. Use (val, i, node) for ties.

Heap / Priority Queue · Coding question

Find Median from Data Stream

LeetCode 295HardTwo heaps (low max-heap + high min-heap)Optimal add O(log n), median O(1)
In plain words

low (max-heap) holds the smaller half, high (min-heap) the larger half. The median sits on top of them.

The problem

Design a class with add_num(num) and find_median(), where numbers arrive one at a time. The median of an even count is the average of the two middle values.

Inputadd 1, add 2, median, add 3, median
Output1.5, 2.0

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
How many calls?Up to 5·10⁴, so sorting on each median call is too slow.
Return type?Float.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 5 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Sorted list with bisect.insort: finding the median is O(1), but inserting into a Python list is O(n). Fine for small inputs; say it first.

Hint 2

Two heaps. Split the numbers into a lower half and an upper half: - low: a max-heap of the smaller half (top = largest of the small numbers); - high: a min-heap of the larger half (top = smallest of the big numbers).

Hint 3

Keep two rules: every number in low ≤ every number in high, and the sizes differ by at most one (let low hold the extra). Then the median is low's top (odd count) or the average of both tops (even count).

Hint 4

Adding a number in three moves: push into low; move low's top to high (this enforces the ordering rule); if high is now bigger, move its top back to low (this enforces the size rule). Each move is O(log n).

Hint 5

Why interviewers ask this: it tests whether you can maintain an invariant across operations. Say the two invariants explicitly.

Say it like this

I'll keep two heaps: a max-heap of the lower half and a min-heap of the upper half, with two invariants: everything in low is ≤ everything in high, and low has the same size or one more. Follow-up questions they ask next

Sliding-window median (LeetCode 480)?

Two heaps plus lazy deletion (a dict of values to remove when they surface at a top), or a sorted container.

Approximate median over billions of values?

Use a quantile sketch (t-digest, KLL). Athena's approx_percentile and Spark's percentile_approx are built on this idea.

Connect it to your AWS work

Exact medians are expensive at scale because they need ordering. That is why warehouses offer APPROX_PERCENTILE: it trades a small error for streaming, mergeable summaries, the distributed cousin of this two-heap structure.

Remember it in one line

Low half = max-heap, high half = min-heap, sizes within 1. Median from the tops.

Intervals & Sessionisation

Problems about time ranges: overlapping meetings, concurrent jobs, user sessions. The first step is almost always "sort by start time".

▬
Think of it like this

A meeting-room calendar. Once meetings are listed in order of start time, any clash shows up between neighbours, and a room becomes free as soon as its last meeting ends.

Almost every interval problem starts with sorting by start (or by end for greedy selection). After that, one sweep is enough, sometimes with a heap of end times to know when resources free up.

overlapmerge rangesmeeting rooms / concurrencysessions / gapsvalidity ranges (SCD2)

The template

Common mistakes

  • Not sorting first.
  • Forgetting max when one interval is nested inside another.
  • Unclear whether touching intervals ([1,2] and [2,3]) overlap: ask.

Deeper notes

Merge overlapping intervals

After sorting by start, an interval overlaps the previous one if it starts before the previous one ends.

Maximum overlap at any moment

"How many rooms do we need?" or "what is the peak number of concurrent Glue jobs?" Keep a min-heap of end times for the intervals currently running.

Sessionisation: the DE classic

Split each user's clickstream into sessions. A new session starts when the gap since the user's previous event exceeds 30 minutes.

Connect the dots

In SQL the same logic is LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user ORDER BY ts), a flag when the gap exceeds 30 minutes, then a running SUM(flag) as the session ID. Merge intervals is how SCD Type 2 validity ranges are collapsed. If you have worked with Quantum Metric or any clickstream feed, use it as your story here.

Meeting Rooms

LeetCode 252EasySort by start, check neighboursOptimal O(n log n)
In plain words

After sorting by start time, any clash must be between a meeting and the very next one.

The problem

Given meeting time intervals [start, end], return True if one person can attend all of them (no two meetings overlap). A meeting ending at 10 and one starting at 10 do not overlap.

Inputintervals = [[0, 30], [5, 10], [15, 20]]
OutputFalse
Inputintervals = [[7, 10], [2, 4]]
OutputTrue

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Does end == next start count as overlap?No, [1, 2] and [2, 3] are fine.
Sorted input?No.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 3 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Brute force: compare every pair for overlap: two intervals a, b overlap when a.start < b.end and b.start < a.end. O(n²).

Hint 2

Sort by start time. After sorting, if any meeting overlaps another, it overlaps its immediate neighbour. Why: if meeting i overlaps some later meeting j, then meeting i+1 starts no later than j, so it starts before i ends too. So you only need to compare each meeting with the next one.

Hint 3

This "sort first, then only compare neighbours" step is the opening move of nearly every interval problem.

Intervals · Coding question

Merge Intervals

LeetCode 56MediumSort by start, extend or append★ Core 40Optimal O(n log n)
In plain words

Sort by start. If the next interval starts before the current block ends, stretch the block. Otherwise start a new block.

The problem

Given a list of intervals, merge all overlapping intervals and return the non-overlapping result.

Inputintervals = [[1, 3], [2, 6], [8, 10], [15, 18]]
Output[[1, 6], [8, 10], [15, 18]]
Inputintervals = [[1, 4], [4, 5]]
Output[[1, 5]]
Touching intervals merge here.

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Do touching intervals merge?Yes, [1, 4] and [4, 5] → [1, 5].
Sorted input?No.
Can I modify the input?Prefer not; I'll sort a copy.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 4 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Sort by start. Then overlapping intervals are consecutive, and you can sweep once.

Hint 2

Sweep with a result list. For each interval: - If it starts at or before the end of the last merged interval, they overlap: extend the last one's end to max(last_end, cur_end). - Otherwise it starts a new merged interval: append it.

Hint 3

The max matters: [1, 10] followed by [2, 3]: the second one is fully inside, so the end must stay 10, not become 3. Forgetting max is the most common bug.

Hint 4

Why sorting is needed: without it, an interval that merges with something seen long ago would be missed.

Intervals arrive in a stream?

Keep merged intervals in a sorted structure and merge each new one with its neighbours (see Insert Interval).

Merge, then sum end - start over the merged list.

Connect it to your AWS work

Merge intervals is how you collapse SCD validity ranges, compute total machine uptime from overlapping status windows, or combine overlapping maintenance windows. In SQL it is the gaps-and-islands technique with LAG and a running sum.

Remember it in one line

Sort by start. start ≤ last.end → last.end = max(last.end, end); else append.

Insert Interval

LeetCode 57MediumThree phases: before, overlap, afterOptimal O(n)
In plain words

The list is already sorted, so one pass in three phases is enough.

The problem

Given a list of non-overlapping intervals sorted by start, insert new_interval and merge if needed. Return the result.

Inputintervals = [[1, 3], [6, 9]], new = [2, 5]
Output[[1, 5], [6, 9]]
Inputintervals = [[1, 2], [3, 5], [6, 7], [8, 10], [12, 16]], new = [4, 8]
