Edge cases to test

  • Missing or non-numeric amount (skipped and counted).
  • True as an amount (bool is a subclass of int, so it must be rejected explicitly).
  • Negative amounts (refunds).
  • Empty input.

Test it yourself

Paste a solution plus the helpers into a .py file and run these checks. Every solution here has been run against them.

Say it like this

"This is a GROUP BY with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX. Rather than scanning the data once per group, I do one pass with a dict from group key to an accumulator of count, total, min and max, and derive the average at the end, since sum and count can be merged but averages can't. Bad amounts are skipped and counted, including booleans, which Python treats as ints. O(n) time, O(groups) memory."

Follow-up questions they ask next

Data split across 100 files processed in parallel?

Compute accumulators per file, then merge: add counts and totals, take min of mins and max of maxes, then derive avg. That is how Spark's partial aggregation works.

Add median?

Medians are not mergeable; keep all values per group (memory heavy) or use an approximate quantile sketch.

Connect it to your AWS work

Mergeable aggregates (count, sum, min, max) are why Spark can aggregate before the shuffle (partial aggregation) and why AVG is computed as SUM / COUNT under the hood. Explaining that shows you understand distributed execution, not just Python.

Remember it in one line

dict[group] = {count, total, min, max}; avg = total / count at the end. Count bad rows.

DE Python Problems · Coding question

Batch Records by Count and Size

MediumGenerator with two limitsOptimal O(n)
In plain words

Fill a batch greedily. If the next record would exceed the count OR the byte limit, send the current batch first. Never forget the last batch.

The problem

Write a generator batch_records(records, max_count, max_bytes) that groups an iterable of byte strings into lists for an API call. Each batch must have at most max_count records and at most max_bytes total bytes. A single record larger than max_bytes must raise ValueError. Preserve order.

Input[b"aaaa", b"bb", b"cccccc", b"d"], max_count = 3, max_bytes = 8
Output[[b"aaaa", b"bb"], [b"cccccc", b"d"]]
Adding cccccc to the first batch would make 12 bytes.

Clarify before you code

Ask these out loud first. The right column is what to assume if the interviewer says "you decide".

AskAssume
Why two limits?Real APIs have both, for example Kinesis PutRecords: 500 records and 5 MB per call; Firehose PutRecordBatch: 500 records and 4 MB (check current docs, limits change).
Oversized single record?Raise; it can never be sent.
Input size?Unbounded stream, so use a generator.
Practise like the real round. Say the brute force out loud, then look for the repeated work. Open a hint only when stuck for 3–5 minutes.

Hints 5 steps from naive to optimal

Hint 1

Greedy packing: keep adding records to the current batch until the next record would break either limit; then yield the batch and start a new one with that record.

Hint 2

Check before adding, not after: compute whether current_bytes + len(rec) > max_bytes or len(batch) == max_count. If either is true, flush first.

Hint 3

Do not forget the last batch: after the loop, yield whatever is left (if non-empty). Forgetting this silently loses the tail of the data, the most common bug.

Hint 4

Generator: yields one batch at a time, so memory is one batch no matter how large the input is.

Hint 5

Brute force for contrast: materialise everything, then slice by count only, which can violate the byte limit and uses O(n) memory.

OptimalGreedy generator with both limitsO(n)≈ 10,000 steps · instant

Slice by count only (wrong on bytes) Brute force

Chunks of max_count, ignoring the size limit. Shown to explain why it fails.

Time O(n)Space O(n)

Fails the requirement: a batch of 3 small-count records can still exceed the byte limit. Mention it to show you considered both limits.

Greedy generator with both limits Optimal

Flush the current batch before a record that would break either limit.

Edge cases to test

  • Empty input → no batches.
  • Record exactly max_bytes.
  • Record larger than max_bytes → ValueError.
  • Count limit reached before the byte limit.

Test it yourself

Paste a solution into a .py file and run these checks. Every solution here has been run against them.

Say it like this

"I'll write a generator that greedily fills a batch. Before adding a record, I check whether it would exceed the count or the byte limit; if so I yield the current batch and start a new one. A single record larger than the byte limit raises, since it can never be sent. After the loop I yield the last partial batch so no data is lost. O(n) time and memory for only one batch."

Follow-up questions they ask next

Kinesis returns some failed records in a batch?

Read FailedRecordCount and the per-record ErrorCode, collect the failed ones, and retry only those with exponential backoff.

Bytes measured after JSON encoding?

Encode each record once (json.dumps(r).encode()), use that length, and send the encoded bytes.

Connect it to your AWS work

Every write to Kinesis, Firehose, SQS (send_message_batch: 10 messages) or DynamoDB (batch_write_item: 25 items) needs exactly this batching, plus a retry for partial failures.

Remember it in one line

Flush before a record breaks count OR bytes; yield the tail; reject oversized records.

Easy		heapq is a min-heap → push −x for a max-heap; negate when reading.O(n log n)O(n)
Kth Largest Element in an Array LC 215
Medium		k largest → MIN-heap of size k; pop when len > k; answer is heap[0].O(n log k)O(k)
K Closest Points to Origin LC 973
Medium		k smallest → MAX-heap of size k (push −dist). Compare squared distances.O(n log k)O(k)
Merge k Sorted Lists LC 23
Hard		Heap of k heads: pop smallest, attach, push its next. Use (val, i, node) for ties.O(N log k)O(k)
Find Median from Data Stream LC 295
Hard		Low half = max-heap, high half = min-heap, sizes within 1. Median from the tops.add O(log n), median O(1)O(n)

Intervals

ProblemKey ideaTimeSpace
Meeting Rooms LC 252
Easy		Sort by start; overlap exists iff some cur.start < prev.end.O(n log n)O(n) for the sorted copy
Merge Intervals LC 56
Medium		Sort by start. start ≤ last.end → last.end = max(last.end, end); else append.O(n log n)O(n)
Insert Interval LC 57
Medium		Sorted input: copy before (end < start), absorb overlap (start ≤ end), copy after.O(n)O(n)
Non-overlapping Intervals LC 435
Medium		Keep the most = sort by END, keep if start ≥ last kept end. Removed = the rest.O(n log n)O(n) for the sorted copy
Meeting Rooms II LC 253
Medium		Rooms = peak overlap. Sort by start; heap of end times; pop if heap[0] ≤ start; push end.O(n log n)O(n)

Trees

ProblemKey ideaTimeSpace
Maximum Depth of Binary Tree LC 104
Easy		Answer(node) = combine(answer(left), answer(right)). Depth = 1 + max(l, r); None → 0.O(n)O(h), h = height
Invert Binary Tree LC 226
Easy		Swap children at every node: root.left, root.right = invert(right), invert(left).O(n)O(h)
Binary Tree Level Order Traversal LC 102
Medium		BFS: for _ in range(len(queue)) → that's one level.O(n)O(w), w = widest level
Validate Binary Search Tree LC 98
Medium		Pass (low, high) down: left gets (low, val), right gets (val, high). Children-only checks are wrong.O(n)O(h)
Diameter of Binary Tree LC 543
Easy		DFS returns height; at each node best = max(best, lh + rh).O(n)O(h)
Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree LC 236
Medium		Return found node up. Hits from both sides → this node is the LCA; else pass up left or right.O(n)O(h)

Graphs

ProblemKey ideaTimeSpace
Number of Islands LC 200
Medium		Grid = graph. Each unseen land cell starts a BFS/DFS that marks its whole island; count the starts.O(rows · cols)O(rows · cols)
Rotting Oranges LC 994
Medium		All sources in the queue first; BFS level by level; each level = one minute.O(rows · cols)O(rows · cols)
Course Schedule LC 207
Medium		Edge pre → course. Kahn's: take in-degree-0 nodes; all taken ⇔ no cycle.O(V + E)O(V + E)
Course Schedule II (Topological Order) LC 210
Medium		Kahn's: queue in-degree-0; pop → append to order → decrement dependents. Short order ⇒ cycle.O(V + E)O(V + E)
Number of Connected Components LC 323
Medium		Union-Find: components = n − successful unions. find with path compression; union by size.O(E · α(n)) ≈ O(E)O(V)

Dynamic Programming

ProblemKey ideaTimeSpace
Climbing Stairs LC 70
Easy		DP recipe: state, transition, base case, order. ways(i) = ways(i−1) + ways(i−2).O(n)O(1)
House Robber LC 198
Medium		best(i) = max(skip: best(i−1), take: nums[i] + best(i−2)).O(n)O(1)
Maximum Subarray (Kadane) LC 53
Medium		cur = max(x, cur + x); best = max(best, cur). Init with nums[0].O(n)O(1)
Coin Change LC 322
Medium		dp[0] = 0; dp[x] = 1 + min(dp[x − c]). Greedy fails on [1, 3, 4] → 6.O(amount · k)O(amount)
Longest Increasing Subsequence LC 300
Medium		dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j] for smaller earlier j). Fast: tails + bisect_left, len(tails).O(n log n)O(n)
Longest Common Subsequence LC 1143
Medium		Match → dp[i−1][j−1] + 1; else max(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]). Zero row/column.O(m · n)O(m · n)

DE Python Problems

ProblemKey ideaTimeSpace
Latest Record per Key (Dedupe)
Easy		dict[id] = record if (updated_at, seq) is newer. ROW_NUMBER() = 1 in one pass.O(n)O(u), u = unique ids
Flatten Nested JSON
Medium		JSON is a tree. Stack of (path, value): containers push children, leaves are stored.O(total nodes)O(width) stack + output
CDC Diff Between Two Snapshots
Medium		Index both by key: inserts = new − old, deletes = old − new, updates = shared keys with different hash.O(n + m) (plus sorting the output)O(n + m)
Top K Error IPs From Access Logs
Medium		Regex-parse lazily, count bad lines, Counter of 5xx per IP, nsmallest(k, key=(−count, ip)).O(n + u log k)O(u), u = unique IPs
Sessionize Clickstream Events
Medium		Sort by (user, ts). New user → 1; gap > 30 min → +1. SQL: LAG + running SUM.O(n log n)O(n)
Find Missing Dates in a Daily Load
Easy		missing = {every day from min to max} − {loaded days}.O(n + d log d)O(n + d)
Merge K Sorted Files Lazily
Medium		Heap of (ts, stream_idx, rec): pop → yield → push next from that stream. O(N log k), O(k) memory.O(N log k)O(k)
Schedule Pipeline Jobs Into Parallel Stages
Medium		Kahn's by levels: in-degree-0 = stage; decrement dependents → next stage; leftovers = cycle.O(V + E) (+ sorting inside stages)O(V + E)
LRU Cache LC 146
Medium		Hash map + doubly linked list. Python: OrderedDict.move_to_end and popitem(last=False).O(1) per operationO(capacity)
Sliding-Window Rate Limiter
Medium		deque per user: pop timestamps ≤ ts − window; allow if len < limit, then append ts.O(1) amortised per callO(users × limit)
GROUP BY Without Pandas
Easy		dict[group] = {count, total, min, max}; avg = total / count at the end. Count bad rows.O(n)O(g), g = number of groups
Batch Records by Count and Size
Medium		Flush before a record breaks count OR bytes; yield the tail; reject oversized records.O(n)O(one batch)

Study Plan & Playbook

What to practise, in what order, how to make it stick, and how to run the 45 minutes of the actual round.

· Open the Practice hub and switch on "Core 40 only".

If you only have one week: the core 40

These cover every pattern at least once and include the questions DE interviewers ask most. Solve each from a blank file, then say the explanation out loud.

The full 4-week plan (about 1.5–2 hours a day)

WeekLearnPractise
1How to think, Python core lessons, verbal questionsAll of Arrays & Hashing and Two Pointers (14 problems). Answer 5 verbal questions out loud per day.
2Sliding window, stack, binary search, linked list pattern lessonsThose four groups (23 problems). Re-solve week 1's problems you marked hard.
3Heap, intervals, trees, graphs, DP pattern lessonsThose five groups (27 problems). Write topological sort and merge-k from memory until each takes under 10 minutes.
4DE problems, concurrency, boto3All 12 DE problems, then daily timed mocks: one DSA medium + one DE problem in 45 minutes, spoken out loud. Read the revision sheet every evening.

How to make it stick: spaced repetition

  1. Day 0: solve it (with help if needed). Write the one-line hook in a notebook.
  2. Day 2: re-solve from a blank file without looking. If you fail, read the "How to think" section again, not the code.
  3. Day 7: re-solve against a 20-minute timer, speaking out loud.
  4. Day 21: just recall the approach from the hook and say the complexity. Code it only if you hesitate.

Understanding why the optimal approach works (the "How to think" section) is what lets you solve new variations in the interview. Memorised code without the reasoning collapses under a small twist.

Running the 45-minute round

MinutesDoSay
0–5Restate, clarify, write an example and an edge case"Just to confirm… Can the input be empty? Is it sorted?"
5–10Brute force + complexity, then the optimised idea + complexity"The simple way is O(n²). The repeated work is …, so a hash map gets it to O(n). Shall I code that?"
10–30Code with clear names; handle edge cases first"I'm using a deque here because I pop from the front."
30–38Trace the example, run edge cases, fix bugs"Let me trace this with the example… i = 0, seen is empty…"
38–45Final complexity, scale, your questions"O(n) time, O(n) space. At 100 GB I'd partition by id in Spark and apply the same logic per partition."

Mistakes that cost senior candidates offers

  • Coding immediately without clarifying, even if the code ends up right.
  • Long silences. Think out loud, even when unsure.
  • Jumping to a clever optimal solution without stating the brute force, then getting stuck with nothing working.
  • Not stating Big-O, or getting x in list wrong (it is O(n)).
  • Not testing: saying "I think it works" instead of tracing an example.
  • Reaching for pandas or Spark when the question is clearly about plain Python logic.
  • Never connecting the answer to real systems. At 6 years, that link is part of what you are hired for.

The day before

  • Read the revision sheet once, slowly.
  • Re-read How to think, especially the six levers and the "at scale" table.
  • Solve two easy problems quickly to warm up, nothing new or hard.
  • Prepare two short stories from your own pipelines where you used these ideas (a dedupe before MERGE, a DAG ordering issue, a memory problem fixed with streaming). Interviewers love it when coding answers connect to real experience.
  • Sleep. Tired brains make off-by-one errors.
